body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Accuracy of medication histories taken by pharmacy technicians and pharmacists in the emergency department: a paired comparison","authors":"Bamidele-Frost C, Nordgren-Sato E, Ruiz-Okafor L","year":2018,"venue":"Hospital Pharmacy Research","doi":"10.5555/hpr.2018.0412","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"For 240 adult admissions through one emergency department, a pharmacy technician and a pharmacist each took a best possible medication history, blind to each other. Against a reference history compiled by a second pharmacist, technicians recorded 91 percent of medications correctly and pharmacists 93 percent. Omissions of as-needed and over-the-counter medicines were the most common errors for both groups. Technicians took a median of 18 minutes per history and pharmacists 15 minutes. The study did not examine reconciliation at discharge or transfer."},{"title":"Pharmacy technician-led discharge medication reconciliation on medical wards: discrepancies detected and pharmacist workload","authors":"Hollis-Amankwah D, Petersen-Iyer R","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Pharmacy Technician Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"On three medical wards, trained technicians compared discharge prescriptions with the admission medication history and the inpatient chart for 1,120 discharges over nine months, and referred discrepancies to a pharmacist. Technicians identified at least one unintentional discrepancy in 34 percent of discharges; pharmacists confirmed 88 percent of the discrepancies referred. Technicians spent a median of 11 minutes per discharge, and most referrals concerned omitted or duplicated medicines. Pharmacist time spent on discharge reconciliation fell by about 60 percent, and pharmacists reported more time for ward rounds. No patient outcomes were measured."},{"title":"Training and supervision models for pharmacy technicians in medication reconciliation: a review of programme descriptions","authors":"Grayson-Obi M, Laurent-Kimura T, Adjei-Sorensen P","year":2021,"venue":"Pharmacy Education and Training","doi":"10.5555/pet.2021.0266","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We identified 46 published and unpublished descriptions of programmes that train pharmacy technicians to take medication histories or reconcile medications. Training ranged from a four-hour workshop to a 12-week accredited course, and 29 programmes required a competency assessment before independent practice. Supervision models included pharmacist review of every history, review of a sample, and review only of flagged discrepancies. Only 11 programmes described how competence was maintained over time, and discharge reconciliation was part of 9 programmes. Few programmes described how supervision was adapted for night or weekend work."},{"title":"Scope of practice for pharmacy technicians in medication reconciliation: a comparison of regulatory frameworks","authors":"Vasquez-Holm A, Oyedele-Brandt S","year":2019,"venue":"Pharmacy Regulation Review","providerType":"report","abstract":"We compared regulations and professional guidance on pharmacy technicians' roles in medication reconciliation across 14 jurisdictions. All allowed regulated technicians to collect medication histories, but only 5 allowed technicians to compare lists and document discrepancies at discharge without a pharmacist present, and none allowed technicians to resolve discrepancies with prescribers. Requirements for registration and training differed widely. Some jurisdictions required a named supervising pharmacist on site, while others accepted remote supervision. The authors note that local policy must be checked against the current regulation, which changed in 4 jurisdictions during the study."},{"title":"Pharmacy technicians in rural hospitals: roles, staffing and medication reconciliation coverage","authors":"Whitaker-Nnadi J, Horvath-Lindberg K","year":2020,"venue":"Rural Health Services Journal","doi":"10.5555/rhsj.2020.0077","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked the pharmacy leads of 118 rural hospitals about technician roles and medication reconciliation coverage. Hospitals where technicians took medication histories reported histories for 78 percent of admissions, against 41 percent where only pharmacists did. Discharge reconciliation by technicians was reported by 12 hospitals. Leads cited limited pharmacist availability at weekends and the distance to supervising pharmacists as the main barriers. Responses were self-reported and not checked against records. The response rate was 61 percent, and hospitals without technicians were less likely to respond."},{"title":"Readmissions after technician-supported discharge reconciliation: a before-after study","authors":"Mbatha-Carrasco E, Quinlan-Oduya F","year":2025,"venue":"Journal of Pharmacy Technician Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"One hospital added technician-supported discharge reconciliation for medical patients and compared 30-day readmissions for 12 months before and 12 months after. Readmission fell from 14.2 to 13.1 percent, a change the authors describe as within the range of secular variation. Medication-related readmissions judged by a pharmacist fell from 2.9 to 2.1 percent. The comparison did not account for a new discharge summary template introduced in the same year. Pharmacists reviewed a tenth of technician reconciliations and agreed with 95 percent of them."},{"title":"Medication reconciliation at care transitions: a map of outcome measures used in 150 evaluations","authors":"Engstrom-Adebayo R, Takahashi-Moreau V","year":2016,"venue":"Medication Safety Outcomes","doi":"10.5555/mso.2016.0155","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We catalogued the outcome measures used in 150 evaluations of medication reconciliation at admission, transfer or discharge. The most common measures were the number of unintentional discrepancies (71 percent of evaluations) and pharmacist-judged potential harm (38 percent); readmission was reported by 22 percent and patient-reported outcomes by 4 percent. Definitions of a discrepancy varied between evaluations, and only 18 percent described how outcome assessors were trained. Evaluations rarely stated who judged potential harm or whether they knew the intervention period. The authors propose a core set of outcomes for future evaluations."}]}
